[108.0, 114.9, 540.0, 126.9]  The albino rats utilized for this study were originally received in good health from
[108.0, 135.6, 540.0, 147.6]  Charles River Laboratories, Inc., Portage, MI and transferred from the WIL Research
[108.0, 156.3, 540.0, 168.3]  stock colony on 25 June 2013. The rats were inspected by a qualified technician upon
[108.0, 174.5, 540.0, 189.0]  receipt, weighed, and uniquely identified by a Monel® metal ear tag displaying the
[108.0, 197.7, 540.0, 209.7]  permanent identification number after receipt at WIL Research. The rats were acclimated
[108.0, 218.4, 539.9, 230.4]  to laboratory conditions for a minimum of 5 days. During this period, each animal was
[108.0, 239.1, 501.9, 251.1]  observed twice daily for mortality and changes in general appearance or behavior.
[108.0, 269.2, 415.5, 283.2]  3.4. METHOD OF TEST SUBSTANCEADMINISTRATION
[108.0, 291.0, 539.9, 303.0]  The rats were fasted overnight prior to dosing. Food was returned approximately 4 hours
[108.0, 311.6, 540.0, 323.6]  after dosing. One group of 3 female albino rats was administered the test substance once
[108.0, 332.2, 540.0, 344.2]  orally via gavage at a level of 2000 mg/kg. Due to no mortality, another 3 female albino
[108.0, 353.0, 540.0, 365.0]  rats were administered the test substance once orally via gavage at a level of 2000 mg/kg
[108.0, 373.6, 539.0, 385.6]  as per OECD Guidelines for Testing of Chemicals, Section 423: Annex 2d (Appendix D).
[108.0, 403.4, 540.0, 415.4]  The test article was dosed undiluted based on its density. The dose volume was
[108.0, 424.0, 540.0, 436.0]  determined by dividing the dose level of 2000 mg/kg, by the density (0.9514g/mL as
[108.0, 444.8, 540.0, 456.8]  listed on the MSDS). Individual doses were calculated based on body weights taken just
[108.0, 465.4, 349.6, 477.4]  prior to dosingand the dosevolume of 2.1 mL/kg.
[108.0, 495.6, 501.9, 509.7]  3.5. ROUTE AND RATIONALE OF TEST SUBSTANCEADMINISTRATION
[108.0, 517.3, 540.0, 529.3]  The selected route of administration for this study was oral (by gavage) in order to
[108.0, 538.0, 540.0, 550.0]  evaluate the acute toxicity of the test substance. This study was intended to provide
[108.0, 558.7, 539.9, 570.7]  information on the health hazards that were likely to arise from a short-term exposure to
[108.0, 579.4, 276.9, 591.4]  the test substance by the oral route.
[108.0, 609.5, 241.1, 623.6]  3.6. ANIMAL HOUSING
[108.0, 631.2, 540.0, 643.2]  All animals were housed individually in clean, stainless steel, wire-mesh cages suspended
[108.0, 651.9, 540.0, 663.9]  above cage board. The animals were maintained by the animal husbandry staff of WIL
[108.0, 672.6, 540.0, 684.6]  Research in accordance with SOPs. The animal facilities at WILResearch are accredited
[290.8, 732.0, 357.1, 744.0]  P a g e 1 0 o f 6 2

[72.0, 491.4, 105.0, 502.5]  Results
[72.0, 514.7, 537.8, 525.7]  Q1. Can olaparib PBPK model provide a reasonable description of the observed DDI effects of olaparib
[72.0, 528.1, 500.7, 539.2]  as a victim (with CYP3A moderators) and a perpetrator (net effect of olaparib on probe CYP3A
[72.0, 541.7, 253.8, 552.7]  substrates and a probe P-gp substrate)?
[72.0, 565.0, 521.4, 576.0]  Olaparib PBPK models have been reviewed by other FDA’s reviewers [4, 5] and were used to support
[72.0, 578.4, 503.0, 589.5]  dosing recommendations of olaparib in the label [3]. The current olaparib PBPK model (Model 6)
[72.0, 591.9, 515.0, 602.9]  reasonably described the plasma concentration-time profile for olaparib tablet following single and
[72.0, 605.3, 526.0, 616.3]  multiple dosing as shown in Table 68. Applicant verified Model 6 using clinical DDI studies with strong
[72.0, 618.7, 532.5, 629.8]  CYP3A inhibitor or inducer (itraconazole and rifampin) as shown in Table 69. The final olaparib Model 6
[72.0, 632.2, 527.2, 643.2]  (Model 6 in Simcyp V15 [1]) is sufficient to predict olaparib PK in patients co-administered with CYP3A
[72.0, 645.6, 531.0, 656.6]  modulators. Appendix Table A2 present the observed and simulated effect of olaparib as a victim (with
[72.0, 659.0, 527.0, 670.1]  CYP3A moderators) and a perpetrator (net effect of olaparib on probe CYP3A substrates, a probe P-gp
[72.0, 672.6, 303.7, 683.6]  substrate, and UGT1A substrate) using the Model 6.

[72.0, 511.6, 540.2, 552.7]  Q1. Can olaparib PBPK model provide a reasonable description of the observed DDI effects of olaparib  / as a victim (with CYP3A moderators) and a perpetrator (net effect of olaparib on probe CYP3A  / substrates and a probe P-gp substrate)?  / 
[72.0, 562.0, 535.0, 683.6]  Olaparib PBPK models have been reviewed by other FDA’s reviewers [4, 5] and were used to support  / dosing recommendations of olaparib in the label [3]. The current olaparib PBPK model (Model 6)  / reasonably described the plasma concentration-time profile for olaparib tablet following single and  / multiple dosing as shown in Table 68. Applicant verified Model 6 using clinical DDI studies with strong  / CYP3A inhibitor or inducer (itraconazole and rifampin) as shown in Table 69. The final olaparib Model 6  / (Model 6 in Simcyp V15 [1]) is sufficient to predict olaparib PK in patients co-administered with CYP3A  / modulators. Appendix Table A2 present the observed and simulated effect of olaparib as a victim (with  / CYP3A moderators) and a perpetrator (net effect of olaparib on probe CYP3A substrates,

[90.0, 119.4, 295.5, 131.4]  2.2 General Clinical Pharmacology
[90.0, 145.2, 522.0, 157.2]  2.2.1 What are the design features of the clinical pharmacology and the
[126.0, 159.0, 412.1, 171.0]  clinical studies used to support dosing or claims?
[90.0, 175.8, 522.0, 187.8]  To support this 505(b)(2) NDA, the Applicant conducted a pivotal bioequivalence study
[90.0, 189.6, 498.9, 201.6]  and a pilot relative bioavailability study. The two studies are summarized in Table 2.
[177.7, 209.4, 434.3, 221.4]  Table 2: Summary of Clinical Pharmacology Studies
[90.0, 224.7, 275.9, 236.7]  Study Description Design
[90.0, 245.4, 499.1, 257.4]  FULV-006- Pivotal BE Parallel design in healthy female volunteers receiving
[90.0, 258.7, 362.3, 271.2]  CP1 study ®
[241.2, 264.2, 479.0, 276.2]  250 mg of FASLODEX (n=133) vs. test product
[241.2, 278.0, 280.0, 290.0]  (n=133)
[90.0, 292.6, 486.9, 304.6]  FULV-005- Pilot BE Parallel study in healthy subjects (n=15 per cohort)
[90.0, 306.4, 474.8, 318.4]  CP1 study comparing PK (up to 126 days) and safety of the
[241.2, 320.2, 435.0, 332.2]  proposed formulation to FASLODEX®.
[90.0, 341.5, 522.0, 353.5]  The Applicant conducted a pilot BE study that was an open label, randomized, two-
[90.0, 355.3, 522.0, 367.3]  treatment, parallel group, single-dose bioequivalence study (FULV-005-CP1) to test the

[90.0, 105.6, 290.8, 117.6]  2.1 General Attributes of the Drug
[90.0, 131.4, 486.1, 143.4]  2.1.1 What are the highlights of the chemistry and physical-chemical

[90.0, 175.8, 169.7, 187.8]  Drug Substance:
[90.0, 195.6, 522.0, 207.6]  Fulvestrant (C H F O S) is a white powder with a molecular weight of 606.77 (Figure
[159.6, 200.5, 207.6, 208.5]  32 47 5 3
[90.0, 209.4, 277.6, 221.4]  1) that is practically insoluble in water.
[224.0, 365.3, 388.0, 377.3]  Figure 1: Structure of Fulvestrant
[90.0, 385.1, 158.3, 397.1]  Drug Product:
[90.0, 404.9, 522.0, 416.9]  Fulvestrant Injection, 250 mg/mL, is a clear colorless to yellow viscous sterile liquid,
[90.0, 418.7, 522.0, 430.7]  supplied in a sterile single-use prefilled syringe for intramuscular injection, each
[90.0, 432.5, 522.0, 444.5]  containing 250 mg fulvestrant. The formulation includes inactive ingredients: alcohol,
[90.0, 444.6, 464.2, 458.3]  benzyl alcohol, polysorbate 80, alpha-tocopherol, and (b) (4) castor oil.
[90.0, 472.1, 522.0, 484.1]  2.1.2 What are the proposed mechanism of action and therapeutic
[126.0, 485.9, 196.7, 497.9]  indications?
[90.0, 502.7, 522.0, 514.7]  Fulvestrant is an antiestrogenic agent that binds – in a competitive manner – to estrogen
[90.0, 516.5, 522.0, 528.5]  receptor (ER). Fulvestrant inhibits the growth of estrogen-sensitive and tamoxifen-
[90.0, 530.3, 297.6, 542.3]  resistant human breast cancer cells in vitro.
[90.0, 550.1, 522.0, 562.1]  Fulvestrant Injection is indicated for the treatment of HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer
[90.0, 563.9, 522.0, 575.9]  in post-menopausal women not previously treated with endocrine therapy and the
[90.0, 576.0, 522.0, 589.7]  treatment of HR+ (b) (4) advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease
[90.0, 591.5, 522.0, 603.5]  progression following endocrine therapy. Fulvestrant is also indicated for the treatment of
[90.0, 605.3, 522.0, 617.3]  HR+/HER2-advanced breast cancer in combination with palbociclib in women with
[90.0, 619.1, 300.9, 631.1]  disease progression after endocrine therapy.
[90.0, 644.9, 480.7, 656.9]  2.1.3 What are the proposed dosages and routes of administration?
[90.0, 661.7, 522.0, 673.7]  Fulvestrant Injection is supplied as two 5 mL prefilled syringes each containing 250 mg
[90.0, 675.5, 522.0, 687.5]  fulvestrant. The recommended dose is 500 mg to be administered intramuscularly into the
[90.0, 689.3, 522.0, 701.3]  buttocks (gluteal area) slowly (1-2 minutes per injection) as two 5 mL injections, one in
[90.0, 703.1, 379.9, 715.1]  each buttock, on days 1, 15, 29 and once monthly thereafter.

[90.0, 73.8, 522.0, 85.8]  Distribution – the apparent volume of distribution at steady-state is approximately 3 to 5
[90.0, 87.6, 522.0, 99.6]  L/kg. Distribution is largely extravascular. Fulvestrant is highly bound (99%) to plasma
[90.0, 101.4, 522.0, 113.4]  proteins; VLDL, LDL, and HDL lipoprotein fractions appear to be the major binding
[90.0, 115.2, 151.0, 127.2]  components.
[90.0, 135.0, 522.0, 147.0]  Metabolism – Fulvestrant biotransformation involves a number of pathways: oxidation,
[90.0, 148.8, 522.0, 160.8]  aromatic hydroxylation, conjugation with glucuronic acid and/or sulphate. The identified
[90.0, 162.6, 522.0, 174.6]  metabolites are either less active or exhibit similar activity to fulvestrant in antiestrogen
[90.0, 176.4, 522.0, 188.4]  models. Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) is the only P-450 isoenzyme involved in the
[90.0, 190.2, 205.6, 202.2]  oxidation of fulvestrant.
[90.0, 210.0, 522.0, 222.0]  Excretion – Fulvestrant is rapidly cleared by the hepatobiliary route with excretion via
[90.0, 223.8, 522.0, 235.8]  the feces (~90%). Renal elimination was negligible (less than 1%). After an
[90.0, 237.6, 522.0, 249.6]  intramuscular injection of 250 mg, the clearance (Mean ± SD) is 690 ± 226 mL/min with
[90.0, 251.4, 243.3, 263.4]  an apparent half-life of 40 days.
[90.0, 277.2, 270.9, 289.2]  2.3 General Biopharmaceutics
[90.0, 303.0, 522.0, 315.0]  2.3.1 What is the relative bioavailability of the proposed product to

[90.0, 73.8, 525.0, 127.2]  Distribution – the apparent volume of distribution at steady-state is approximately 3 to 5  / L/kg. Distribution is largely extravascular. [90.0, 135.0, 525.0, 202.2]  Metabolism  –  Fulvestrant  biotransformation  involves  a  number  of  pathways:  oxidation,  / aromatic hydroxylation, conjugation with glucuronic acid and/or sulphate. The identified  / metabolites are either less active or exhibit similar activity to fulvestrant in antiestrogen  / models. Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP 3A4) is the only P-450 isoenzyme involved in the  / oxidation of fulvestrant. / 
[90.0, 210.0, 525.0, 263.4]  Excretion  –  Fulvestrant  is  rapidly  cleared  by  the  hepatobiliary  route  with  excretion  via  / the  feces  (~90%).  Renal  elimination  was  negligible  (less  than  1%).  After  an  / intramuscular injection of 250 mg, the clearance (Mean ± SD) is 690 ± 226 mL/min with  / an apparent half-life of 40 days. /

[72.0, 307.6, 540.0, 319.6]  A thorough ensemble of alternative bioavailability, absorption, and disposition models were tested.
[72.0, 321.4, 539.9, 333.4]  Linear, logarithmic, and exponential dose-bioavailability relationships were tested; as suggested
[72.0, 335.2, 540.1, 347.2]  by the applicant, an exponential model produced the lowest drop in OFV. Estimation of absorption
[72.0, 349.0, 540.2, 361.0]  rate caused model instability for the reviewer, and therefore was fixed to 200. One, two, and three
[72.0, 362.8, 539.9, 374.8]  compartment models were tested for both parent and metabolite. A two-compartment parent, two
[72.0, 376.6, 540.0, 388.6]  compartment metabolite disposition model fit the data reasonably well. There was a tendency for
[72.0, 390.4, 540.1, 402.4]  the model to under predict concentrations past 24 hrs, indicating the presence of a slowly
[72.0, 404.2, 540.0, 416.2]  equilibrating third compartment. However, the absolute impact (e.g. bias in AUC ) of this
[488.4, 407.9, 497.4, 416.0]  inf
[72.0, 418.0, 539.9, 430.0]  underestimation is comparatively small in magnitude. The fixed effect covariance matrix was
[72.0, 431.8, 539.9, 443.8]  diagonalized, and included terms for F, CL, V1, Q, V2 for the parent, and CL, Q, V1, V2 for the
[72.0, 445.6, 540.1, 457.6]  metabolite. Adding IIV on other PK parameters improved the model fit significantly, as judged by
[72.0, 458.4, 380.9, 471.4]  the ∆OFV, but caused high η-shrinkage and centering problems.
[72.0, 487.0, 539.9, 499.0]  Covariate modeling identified one statistically significant covariate (weight on fraction of parent
[72.0, 500.8, 540.1, 512.8]  converted to metabolite). No clinically significant covariate effect signals were detected (figure
[72.0, 514.6, 121.0, 526.6]  4.1.3.4.1).

[72.0, 75.1, 171.8, 87.1]  Sensitivity Analysis
[72.0, 102.4, 540.0, 114.4]  The internal audit conducted by the applicant did not reveal conclusive evidence of the source or
[72.0, 116.2, 540.1, 128.2]  extent of the sample issues. Possible explanations were provided, such as contamination due to
[72.0, 130.0, 540.1, 142.0]  environmental traces of nebulized product, sample switching, mislabeling, inaccurate sampling
[72.0, 143.8, 539.9, 155.8]  time and/or sampling very close to or immediately after inhalation of test drug. Of importance,
[72.0, 157.6, 540.0, 169.6]  the applicant was unable to exclude that the PK samples collected on Visit 4, 5, 6, and 7 were not
[72.0, 171.4, 540.0, 183.4]  also impacted by sampling issues. Parameter estimates for the sensitivity analysis were provided
[72.0, 185.2, 540.0, 197.2]  by the applicant for Phase III exclusion and for outlier exclusion. No parameter estimates were
[72.0, 199.0, 292.2, 211.0]  supplied for pre-dose concentration inclusion.

[72.0, 477.5, 168.9, 489.5]  Covariate Analysis
[72.0, 504.8, 540.0, 516.8]  Two covariates were identified as being statistically significant in the original revefenacin
[72.0, 518.6, 540.0, 530.6]  population PK model (Phase 2 and 3 data): age on clearance (CL/F) and weight on
[72.0, 532.4, 540.0, 544.4]  intercompartmental clearance (Q/F). Two covariates were identified in the original THRX-195518
[72.0, 546.2, 540.0, 558.2]  population PK model as being statistically significant: age on metabolite clearance (CLmet/F) and
[72.0, 560.0, 539.9, 572.0]  weight on the fraction of revefenacin metabolism that is the formation of THRX-195518 (Fmet).
[72.0, 573.8, 430.2, 585.8]  No covariate was identified as statistically significant in the pooled model.
[72.0, 601.4, 540.1, 613.4]  As discussed above, the covariate analysis for the pooled data is unreliable; as it is possible that
[72.0, 615.2, 539.9, 627.2]  the error in the Phase III data caused invalid base model or covariate selection to be done, which
[72.0, 629.0, 540.0, 641.0]  would propagate to the covariate effects for the pooled estimates. However, the applicant
[72.0, 642.8, 540.1, 654.8]  conducted a sensitivity analysis with Phase II data only. The covariate effects reported using only
[72.0, 656.6, 540.0, 668.6]  Phase II subjects support the results of the pooled analysis (figures 4.1.2.4.5 – 4.1.2.4.8). The
[72.0, 670.4, 539.9, 682.4]  reported covariate effects in Phase 2 subjects suggest no clinically relevant difference in exposure
[72.0, 684.2, 539.9, 696.2]  with respect to age, sex, and weight (all point estimates were within 75-125% for C and AUC).

[72.0, 147.9, 540.0, 159.9]  No heteroscedasticity with respect to time or concentration was noted in the goodness of fit plots.
[72.0, 161.7, 539.9, 173.7]  The model fit individual concentration-time profiles well, and could obtain plausible parameter
[72.0, 175.5, 540.0, 187.5]  estimates within reasonable levels of uncertainty (table 4.1.1.4.1). In the renal impairment study,
[72.0, 189.3, 540.1, 201.3]  two healthy subjects were identified as outliers and excluded from analysis. The excluded subjects
[72.0, 203.1, 540.1, 215.1]  had exposures that were the among the lowest of all studied healthy subjects receiving a 175-mcg
[72.0, 216.9, 385.6, 228.9]  dose (n=64), and subjects with confirmed dosing noncompliance.
[72.0, 244.5, 539.9, 256.5]  Based on fixed effect estimates of CL/F, the model predicts revefenacin AUC in both hepatic and
[72.0, 258.3, 539.9, 270.3]  renal impaired subjects to be within 20% of healthy subjects. The model predicts THRX-195518
[72.0, 272.1, 539.9, 284.1]  AUC to be within 20% of healthy subjects for renal impairment, and predicts a 143% increase of
[72.0, 285.9, 336.5, 297.9]  the metabolite AUC in moderate hepatic impairment.
[168.6, 289.6, 177.6, 297.7]  inf
[72.0, 313.5, 539.8, 325.5]  Based on subsequent NCA and ANOVA analysis of model predicted concentrations from post-
[72.0, 327.3, 540.0, 339.3]  hoc simulations, greater than 200% increases in parent and metabolite AUCs were predicted in
[72.0, 341.1, 540.2, 353.1]  renal impairment. However, after removal of the outliers, exposure ratios as predicted by
[72.0, 354.9, 540.0, 366.9]  NCA/ANOVA analysis (table 4.1.1.4.2, figure 4.1.1.4.1) were approximate to the predictions
[72.0, 368.7, 540.2, 380.7]  based on the population PK model. The model predicted a 184% increase in AUC of the metabolite
[72.0, 382.5, 539.9, 394.5]  in hepatic impairment. Otherwise, all organ impairment effects on were estimated to be less than
[72.0, 396.3, 257.9, 408.3]  twice the exposure of healthy subjects.

[51.0, 451.2, 142.2, 467.2]  1. Introduction
[51.0, 476.3, 134.7, 490.3]  1.1 Objective
[51.0, 496.0, 402.5, 507.0]  This guideline is intended to provide recommendations for the validation of
[51.0, 509.4, 402.5, 520.4]  bioanalytical methods for chemical and biological drug quantification in biological
[51.0, 522.8, 402.5, 533.8]  matrices and their application in the analysis of study samples. Adherence to the
[51.0, 536.2, 402.5, 547.2]  principles presented in this guideline will ensure the quality and consistency of
[51.0, 549.6, 402.5, 560.6]  the bioanalytical data in support of the development and market approval of both
[51.0, 563.0, 184.8, 574.0]  chemical and biological drugs.
[85.0, 576.4, 402.5, 587.4]  The objective of the validation of a bioanalytical method is to demonstrate
[51.0, 589.8, 402.5, 600.8]  that it is suitable for its intended purpose. Changes from the recommendations in
[51.0, 603.2, 402.5, 614.2]  this guideline may be acceptable if appropriate scientific justification is provided.
[51.0, 616.6, 402.5, 627.6]  Applicants are encouraged to consult the relevant regulatory authority regarding
